planting.note: Establish container divisions in saturated soil or standing shallow water in spring once temperatures warm; avoid direct seeding, as germination is unreliable and slow.

directions: Plant divisions directly into wet muck, brackish marsh edges, or shallow standing freshwater, since this large sedge dominates the Everglades and Gulf Coast freshwater-to-brackish marsh transition zone. The saw-toothed leaf margins that give the plant its name can cause skin cuts, so handle with gloves during planting and maintenance. It spreads by rhizome into dense stands that stabilize marsh substrate and provide cover for wading birds, and it tolerates periodic fire and fluctuating water levels once established. Give it full sun and consistently saturated to inundated soil; it does not perform well in average garden beds.

planting.note: Set plugs or rhizome divisions into saturated soil at the brackish or freshwater marsh edge in spring; keep soil consistently wet through establishment.

directions: This triangular-stemmed rush colonizes the mid-marsh zone of Gulf Coast estuaries and freshwater shorelines, where its dense rhizome mats resist erosion and filter runoff before it reaches open water. Historically its tough, pliable stems were split and woven for chair seats and baskets, giving the plant its common name. Plant into consistently wet to seasonally flooded soil in full sun; it tolerates brackish water up to moderate salinity and periodic tidal inundation better than most freshwater sedges. Use it in living-shoreline plantings alongside smooth cordgrass and black needlerush to build a graded marsh transition.

common_name: Seacoast Marsh Elder (Beach Elder, Dune Marsh Elder)

planting.note: Direct seed or set out containerized plants into loose, well-drained beach sand in spring; supplemental watering is needed only until roots reach the water table.

directions: A low, succulent-leaved shrub of the primary and secondary dune zone, seacoast marsh elder grows just landward of sea oats where salt spray and burial by wind-blown sand are constant. Its fleshy gray-green foliage sheds salt efficiently, and its spreading root system helps knit loose dune sand together. Plant in full sun in pure beach sand with no irrigation once established; it is intolerant of rich garden soil or regular watering. Use it as a companion to sea oats and railroad vine in dune restoration plantings, where it fills the low, wind-scoured swales between larger grass clumps.

planting.note: Set out container-grown plants in fall or early spring into deep, loose sand; avoid heavy or poorly drained soils, which quickly rot the roots.

directions: Native to the scrub and stabilized secondary dunes of the Florida Panhandle and Gulf Coast, this rounded evergreen shrub produces silvery, resinous foliage and a showy flush of small yellow flower heads in mid to late fall. It is extremely drought and salt tolerant once rooted, thriving in deep, sterile beach or scrub sand where few other flowering shrubs survive. Give it full sun and sharp drainage, and resist the urge to fertilize or irrigate beyond the first season. It works well massed on dune crests or in xeric coastal gardens where its fall bloom complements late-season grasses like muhly and bluestem.

planting.note: Direct sow onto bare, salty mud or sand at the marsh-upland border after the danger of frost has passed; this species self-seeds readily once established.

directions: This slender, succulent-leaved annual colonizes bare salt pans, marsh borders, and the upper edge of salt marshes where salinity is too high for most other plants, turning reddish-purple in fall as it sets seed. Sow directly onto disturbed saline soil in full sun; it needs no irrigation beyond natural rainfall and actually performs best on the driest, saltiest microsites in a planting. Because it is a true annual, expect it to die back each winter and reseed the following spring in undisturbed soil. Use it as a pioneer species on newly created or restored marsh edges alongside glasswort and saltwort, where its fibrous roots help hold bare salt-flat soil before perennial cordgrass fills in.

planting.note: Plant rooted cuttings or container stock in spring in the dappled shade of maritime hammocks or coastal woodland edges; establish with regular water the first season, then reduce.

directions: A sprawling, semi-woody vine-shrub of Florida and Gulf Coast maritime hammocks, milkberry produces small fragrant white tubular flowers followed by glossy white berries that persist through much of the year and are relished by birds. It scrambles over neighboring shrubs or can be kept as a loose mounding groundcover shrub with occasional pruning. Grow in partial shade to filtered sun in humus-rich, well-drained soil typical of coastal hammock understories, and provide some wind protection when young since it is not a true front-dune plant. Its salt and drought tolerance once established make it useful as a naturalizing understory shrub in restored maritime forest plantings.

planting.note: Set out rooted stem cuttings or container plants into well-drained sandy soil in spring after frost danger passes; water in well and then taper off once roots establish.

directions: Native to the coastal strand and stabilized dunes of peninsular Florida, golden creeper forms a low, mounding evergreen mat with narrow succulent leaves and small yellow-green tubular flowers followed by orange-red fruit. It spreads by trailing stems that root as they touch sand, making it an effective low groundcover for binding dune soil without the height of sea oats or panic grass. Grow in full sun in sharply drained sandy soil and expect excellent tolerance of salt spray, drought, and occasional saltwater flooding. It is frost-tender and best suited to the immediate Gulf and southern Atlantic coast, where it is used in dune stabilization and low-maintenance coastal landscaping.

planting.note: Plant plugs or divisions into consistently moist to saturated soil in spring; ideal for pond margins, rain gardens, and freshwater marsh edges rather than dry beds.

directions: This clump-forming rush grows through the Southeast in wet pine flatwoods, ditches, and the freshwater fringes of brackish marshes, producing wiry blue-green stems topped with small clustered brown flower heads in summer. Plant divisions into damp to saturated soil in full to partial sun; it tolerates both standing water and seasonal drying better than many rushes, making it forgiving in rain gardens and stormwater basins. It rarely needs division or maintenance once established and provides fine winter texture along pond edges. Combine it with pickerelweed and native sedges for a layered freshwater marsh planting that also offers cover for small wetland wildlife.
